vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair with his back straight, hands folded in his lap. At fifty-one, he carries himself with the precision of someone accustomed to order-his tie is perfectly knotted, his shirt unwrinkled. He has been a tax inspector for twenty-three years, a career built on attention to detail and control. But his eyes betray something else entirely.

Seven years ago, Marcus was in a relationship with David, a man he believed he would spend his life with. They had been together for four years when David's drinking escalated. What began as occasional arguments became something darker. Marcus remembers one night in particular-a Tuesday in March-when David came home angry about something Marcus had said at dinner. The argument spiraled quickly. David shoved him against the kitchen counter, then hit him repeatedly across the face and torso. Marcus remembers the sound of his own breathing, the taste of blood, the way his body seemed to separate from his mind.

When it ended, Marcus locked himself in the bathroom. He told himself it was an isolated incident, that David had been drinking, that it wouldn't happen again. But it did. Over the following months, the violence became unpredictable-sometimes weeks of relative calm, then sudden explosions. Marcus found himself constantly vigilant, reading David's mood, trying to anticipate what might set him off. He became hyperaware of his own movements, his words, his tone of voice.

It took him eight months to leave.

That was six years ago, and Marcus has not been in another relationship since. He is married now-to a woman named Priya whom he met through mutual friends-but the marriage feels hollow to him. He loves her, he insists, but he cannot allow himself to be vulnerable with her. When she touches him unexpectedly, he flinches. When she raises her voice during an argument, something inside him contracts with dread. Priya has stopped trying to initiate intimacy. She has stopped asking him to talk about his day.

At work, Marcus is respected but distant. His colleagues describe him as meticulous, almost obsessive about accuracy. What they don't see is that this precision is a form of control-if he can order the numbers, the spreadsheets, the audits perfectly, perhaps he can order his own mind. He works late most nights, finding comfort in the quiet office, the glow of his computer screen.

But the nights are difficult. Marcus sleeps poorly, often waking in a state of panic, his heart racing, convinced that someone is in the room with him. He has nightmares where he is back in that kitchen, or sometimes where the violence is happening to someone else and he cannot stop it. He wakes gasping, and Priya pretends to be asleep.

During the day, he is hypervigilant in ways he cannot fully explain. He positions himself in rooms so his back is to the wall. He notices exits. He startles at sudden noises-a car horn, a raised voice in the hallway-and takes several minutes to calm down. When a junior colleague raised his voice during a meeting last month, Marcus felt his entire body go rigid. He excused himself and spent fifteen minutes in the bathroom, breathing slowly, telling himself he was safe.

Marcus knows something is wrong. He knows that the way he moves through the world is not how other people move through it. But talking about what happened feels impossible. It contradicts everything he believes about himself-that he is competent, in control, capable. That he is a man.
